name: Hardware Security
description: Security of hardware: chips, FPGAs, PUFs, fault injection, and hardware design verification.

ccs.narrative:
Hardware security at CCS has been defined by the speculative-execution revolution and its aftershocks. The 2018-2019 period produced some of the most-cited CCS papers ever: ret2spec (CCS 2018), ZombieLoad (CCS 2019), Fallout (CCS 2019), and SMoTherSpectre (CCS 2019) collectively mapped the transient-execution attack landscape on Intel processors. Screaming Channels (CCS 2018) added an RF-side-channel dimension, and Rendered Insecure (CCS 2018) extended hardware attacks to GPUs. Nemesis (CCS 2018) closed the circle by targeting SGX via interrupt timing.

Fault-injection attacks against neural networks and TEEs formed a parallel track. Practical Fault Attack on Deep Neural Networks (CCS 2018) showed row-hammer style bit flips can misclassify DNN outputs, while VoltJockey: Breaching TrustZone by Software-Controlled Voltage Manipulation over Multi-core Frequencies (CCS 2019) induced faults in TrustZone via software-controlled voltage scaling. One Glitch to Rule Them All: Fault Injection Attacks Against AMD's Secure Encrypted Virtualization (CCS 2021) extended glitching to AMD SEV.

Defense research moved toward formal verification of hardware contracts. InSpectre: Breaking and Fixing Microarchitectural Vulnerabilities by Formal Analysis (CCS 2020) automated the find-and-fix cycle for Spectre gadgets. Exorcising Spectres with Secure Compilers (CCS 2021) proved that compiler mitigations can be formally sound against an attacker with full microarchitectural knowledge.

milestones.title: ret2spec: Speculative Execution Using Return Stack Buffers
milestones.note: Discovered a Spectre variant exploiting return-stack-buffer misprediction to leak arbitrary memory.

milestones.title: Rendered Insecure: GPU Side Channel Attacks are Practical
milestones.note: Made GPU side-channel attacks practical, leaking sensitive data from graphics and ML compute workloads.

milestones.title: Screaming Channels: When Electromagnetic Side Channels Meet Radio Transceivers
milestones.note: Found that RF transceivers on SoCs broadcast side-channel leakage, enabling wireless key extraction.

milestones.title: Practical Fault Attack on Deep Neural Networks
milestones.note: Demonstrated hardware fault injection can reliably subvert DNN inference results.

milestones.title: ZombieLoad: Cross-Privilege-Boundary Data Sampling
milestones.note: Leaked cross-privilege data by exploiting CPU load-buffer fill behavior during transient execution.

milestones.title: VoltJockey: Breaching TrustZone by Software-Controlled Voltage Manipulation over Multi-core Frequencies
milestones.note: Broke ARM TrustZone isolation using software-controlled CPU voltage to induce exploitable hardware faults.

milestones.title: InSpectre: Breaking and Fixing Microarchitectural Vulnerabilities by Formal Analysis
milestones.note: Automated Spectre gadget detection and repair using formal microarchitectural analysis.

milestones.title: One Glitch to Rule Them All: Fault Injection Attacks Against AMD's Secure Encrypted Virtualization
milestones.note: Broke AMD SEV's memory encryption and register protection with voltage glitch attacks on the secure processor.

ndss.narrative:
Hardware security at NDSS has addressed the full stack from microcontroller memory isolation to GPU-accelerated enclave extensions. Securing Real-Time Microcontroller Systems through Customized Memory Views (NDSS 2018) demonstrated that even resource-constrained embedded devices can enforce fine-grained privilege separation, establishing a baseline for later IoT-hardening work. SANCTUARY (NDSS 2019) moved up to ARM TrustZone, extending its applicability to user-space enclaves on commodity mobile SoCs.

The 2020–2022 period was dominated by side-channel and voltage-based threats. ConTExT (NDSS 2020) proposed a generic mitigation for Spectre by making sensitive data context-dependent; Evading Voltage-Based Intrusion Detection on Automotive CAN (NDSS 2021) showed how attackers can spoof ECU voltage fingerprints; and GhostTalk (NDSS 2022) demonstrated power-line eavesdropping on smartphone voice systems. These papers collectively showed that physical observability of hardware is a durable attack surface.

By 2024–2025 the frontier had moved to heterogeneous trusted computing. CAGE (NDSS 2024) proposed GPU extensions to ARM CCA, enabling confidential GPU workloads; CounterSEVeillance (NDSS 2025) showed that performance counters leak sensitive state from AMD SEV-SNP protected VMs; and electromagnetic interference attacks on power inverters (ReThink, NDSS 2025) demonstrated that the power grid's cyber-physical interface is as vulnerable as any software stack. The community's focus has broadened from CPU microarchitecture to the entire silicon ecosystem.

milestones.title: Securing Real-Time Microcontroller Systems through Customized Memory View Switching
milestones.note: Secures real-time microcontrollers with customized memory-view switching to provide isolation without sacrificing real-time guarantees.

milestones.title: SANCTUARY: ARMing TrustZone with User-space Enclaves
milestones.note: Extends ARM TrustZone with isolated user-space enclaves so developers can run protected applications without secure-world code.

milestones.title: ConTExT: A Generic Approach for Mitigating Spectre
milestones.note: Proposes ConTExT, a generic processor and software defense that prevents secret leakage through Spectre-style transient execution.

milestones.title: Evading Voltage-Based Intrusion Detection on Automotive CAN
milestones.note: Demonstrates attacks evading voltage-based ECU fingerprinting intrusion detection on automotive CAN buses.

milestones.title: GhostTalk: Interactive Attack on Smartphone Voice System Through Power Line
milestones.note: Injects inaudible voice commands into smartphone voice systems through the power line interface interactively.

milestones.title: Paralyzing Drones via EMI Signal Injection on Sensory Communication Channels
milestones.note: Shows electromagnetic interference injection on IMU sensor communication channels can paralyze drones by corrupting attitude-control data.

milestones.title: CAGE: Complementing Arm CCA with GPU Extensions
milestones.note: CAGE extends Arm Confidential Computing Architecture to provide confidential computing for GPU workloads.

milestones.title: On the Realism of LiDAR Spoofing Attacks against Autonomous Driving Vehicle at High Speed and Long Distance
milestones.note: Evaluates realism of LiDAR spoofing attacks against autonomous vehicles at high speed and long distance.

sp.narrative:
Hardware security at IEEE S&P tracks threats to and from physical computing substrates. The 2018 baseline combined power side-channels with memory attacks: FPGA-Based Remote Power Side-Channel Attacks (S&P 2018) demonstrated cloud-based power analysis, and Another Flip in the Wall of Rowhammer Defenses (S&P 2018) bypassed state-of-the-art DRAM refresh mitigations. Grand Pwning Unit: Accelerating Microarchitectural Attacks with the GPU (S&P 2018) widened the attack surface to GPU-accelerated cache timing.

2019 elevated hardware security to a core S&P theme. Spectre Attacks: Exploiting Speculative Execution (S&P 2019) revealed that virtually every modern CPU's performance optimization undermines its isolation guarantees—the highest-cited paper in this dataset. RIDL: Rogue In-Flight Data Load (S&P 2019), Port Contention for Fun and Profit (S&P 2019), and Exploiting Correcting Codes: On the Effectiveness of ECC Memory Against Rowhammer Attacks (S&P 2019) followed, collectively establishing 2019 as the peak year for microarchitectural attack disclosures.

The 2020 papers pursued both new attack surfaces and systematic defenses. Plundervolt (S&P 2020) combined software-accessible voltage control with SGX fault injection, TRRespass (S&P 2020) defeated DRAM's TRR countermeasure, and LVI: Hijacking Transient Execution through Microarchitectural Load Value Injection (S&P 2020) inverted the direction of transient execution attacks. SoK: Understanding the Prevailing Security Vulnerabilities in TrustZone-assisted TEE Systems (S&P 2020) catalogued the TEE attack landscape.

From 2021-2024, hardware security papers increasingly addressed emerging platforms: PLATYPUS (S&P 2021) via RAPL power interfaces, BLACKSMITH (S&P 2022) via frequency-domain Rowhammer, and a growing body of work on RISC-V, ARM, and AMD SEV security as these architectures displaced Intel's monopoly in research targets.

milestones.note: revealed that speculative execution breaks security isolation on virtually all modern CPUs

uss.narrative:
The earliest work in this list is dominated by the microarchitectural reckoning of 2018. Meltdown: Reading Kernel Memory from User Space (USENIX 2018) showed that the fundamental assumption underpinning system security — that kernel memory is isolated from user processes — could be broken by abusing speculative execution and CPU cache timing. The same venue and year piled on related cracks in isolation: Translation Leak-aside Buffer (USENIX 2018) defeated cache side-channel protections via the TLB, and Malicious Management Unit (USENIX 2018) argued that stopping cache attacks in software was far harder than assumed. Alongside these CPU attacks, A Bad Dream: Subverting Trusted Platform Module While You Are Sleeping (USENIX 2018) showed even dedicated trust hardware (the TPM) could be subverted through power management.

The next phase widened the attack surface and started building defenses. On the offense side, SPOILER (USENIX 2019) connected speculative load hazards to Rowhammer and cache attacks, and the community pushed into machine learning hardware with Terminal Brain Damage (USENIX 2019), followed by DeepHammer (USENIX 2020), which depleted neural network accuracy through targeted chains of DRAM bit flips. Researchers also broadened beyond pure microarchitecture: Light Commands (USENIX 2020) injected audio into voice assistants using lasers, and USBFuzz (USENIX 2020) fuzzed USB drivers via device emulation. Defensive and verification work matured in parallel — ScatterCache (USENIX 2019) randomized cache sets to thwart side channels, VRASED (USENIX 2019) delivered a formally verified hardware/software co-design for remote attestation, and HardFails (USENIX 2019) gave early insight into why software-exploitable hardware bugs evade detection. In-process isolation primitives like IMIX (USENIX 2018), Donky (USENIX 2020), and the critical PKU Pitfalls (USENIX 2020) traced an arms race over fine-grained memory protection keys.

By 2021-2022 the field professionalized into systematic analysis and automation. VoltPillager (USENIX 2021) brought hardware fault injection to bear on Intel SGX via the voltage interface, while transient-execution research turned reflective with DOLMA (USENIX 2021), Rage Against the Machine Clear (USENIX 2021), and RETBLEED (USENIX 2022), which revived speculative code execution through return instructions. Rowhammer itself proved relentless: SMASH (USENIX 2021) hammered from JavaScript despite TRR mitigations, Half-Double (USENIX 2022) reached two rows away, and ZenHammer (USENIX 2024) carried the attack onto AMD Zen platforms — a multi-year cat-and-mouse against DRAM defenses. New channels kept emerging too, from the ring interconnect in Lord of the Ring(s) (USENIX 2021) to AMD Prefetch Attacks (USENIX 2022) and ÆPIC Leak (USENIX 2022). Crucially, the toolset shifted from one-off discoveries toward automated discovery and verification — Osiris (USENIX 2021) automatically found microarchitectural side channels, and TheHuzz (USENIX 2022) fuzzed processors against golden-reference models to surface exploitable hardware bugs. The trajectory across these venues runs from a few shocking isolation breaks, through an explosion of attack surfaces and ad-hoc defenses, to a current state defined by systematic, automated hunting for hardware vulnerabilities and an unfinished battle over DRAM and speculative execution.

milestones.title: Meltdown: Reading Kernel Memory from User Space
milestones.note: the landmark break of kernel-user memory isolation that launched the modern microarchitectural security era

milestones.title: Terminal Brain Damage: Exposing the Graceless Degradation in Deep Neural Networks Under Hardware Fault Attacks
milestones.note: opened hardware fault attacks against machine learning models, bridging hardware security and ML

milestones.note: showed formally verified hardware/software co-design could deliver trustworthy remote attestation

milestones.note: expanded the field beyond microarchitecture by physically injecting commands into sensors via light

milestones.note: marked the shift from manual discovery to automated hunting of microarchitectural side channels

milestones.note: brought scalable fuzzing and golden-reference verification to processor hardware bug discovery

milestones.note: revived Spectre-class speculative execution attacks through return instructions, defeating deployed mitigations

top4.narrative:
The earliest papers on this list mark the moment when hardware security stopped being a niche concern and became front-page news. In 2018, "Meltdown: Reading Kernel Memory from User Space" (USENIX 2018) and the broader wave of transient-execution work showed that the speculative and out-of-order machinery inside every modern CPU could be turned into a leak, reading memory that hardware isolation was supposed to protect. Alongside it, the same year saw a striking breadth of attack surfaces opened up: remote power side channels on cloud FPGAs ("FPGA-Based Remote Power Side-Channel Attacks", S&P 2018), DRAM bit-flipping defenses being broken ("Another Flip in the Wall of Rowhammer Defenses", S&P 2018), side channels on GPUs ("Rendered Insecure: GPU Side Channel Attacks are Practical", CCS 2018), electromagnetic leakage from radios ("Screaming Channels", CCS 2018), and fault attacks reaching into neural networks ("Practical Fault Attack on Deep Neural Networks", CCS 2018). The throughline is that physical and microarchitectural properties of real chips, long treated as implementation details, were now exploitable primitives.

2019 was the year these threads matured and multiplied. "Spectre Attacks" (S&P 2019) generalized Meltdown's lesson into a whole class of branch-prediction attacks, and a family of microarchitectural data-sampling attacks followed in quick succession across venues: "ZombieLoad" (CCS 2019), "RIDL: Rogue In-Flight Data Load" (S&P 2019), and "Fallout" (CCS 2019), each leaking in-flight data from internal CPU buffers even on supposedly Meltdown-resistant hardware. Researchers also sharpened the underlying tooling and defenses, from making cache attacks more rigorous ("Theory and Practice of Finding Eviction Sets", S&P 2019) to proposing randomized caches ("ScatterCache", USENIX 2019). At the same time the community began turning the lens on the design process itself: "HardFails" (USENIX 2019) studied why hardware bugs slip past verification, and "VRASED" (USENIX 2019) offered a formally verified hardware/software co-design for remote attestation, signaling a shift from finding attacks to building provable defenses.

From 2020 onward the field pushed in two complementary directions: weaponizing the chip's own control knobs, and scaling up both attacks and verification. "Plundervolt" (S&P 2020) and later "PLATYPUS" (S&P 2021) showed that software-exposed voltage and power interfaces could inject faults or leak secrets from inside Intel SGX, while "LVI" (S&P 2020) inverted Spectre by injecting attacker data into a victim's transient execution. Rowhammer kept escalating as each hardware mitigation was bypassed in turn, through "TRRespass" (S&P 2020), "RAMBleed" (S&P 2020, which read rather than just flipped bits), and "BLACKSMITH" (S&P 2022). A distinct and growing strand applied these primitives to machine learning, with "DeepHammer" (USENIX 2020) and "DeepSteal" (S&P 2022) degrading or stealing neural networks via memory faults.

Two trends define where the area stands now. First, the defensive and verification side has caught up: "DifuzzRTL" (S&P 2021) brought differential fuzzing directly to register-transfer-level CPU design to find bugs before fabrication, complementing the verified-design ethos of VRASED and the bug-hunting motivation of HardFails. Second, the attack surface has broadened well beyond the CPU core, spanning physical injection like "Light Commands" (USENIX 2020) and cross-core speculative leaks ("CrossTalk", S&P 2021; "CacheOut", S&P 2021). The net trajectory is clear: what began as isolated microarchitectural curiosities has become a mature discipline that treats every layer of real hardware, from DRAM cells to voltage regulators to RTL design, as part of the attack and defense surface.
